abstract: Mitochondrial aerobic metabolism is thought to play a central role in the mechanisms underlying aging. However, because metabolism scales with body mass, which strongly predicts lifespan, disentangling the relationship between mitochondrial metabolism and lifespan from the shared allometric scaling of both traits with body mass remains a persistent challenge. Here, we address this issue by using a phylogenetically controlled, multivariate Bayesian approach to test whether different mitochondrial traits covary with lifespan independently of body mass, across 41 bird species (maximal lifespan: 6-41 years; body mass: 9 g-13 kg). Our results show that, after controlling for body mass, species maximal lifespan was associated with the cellular control of mitochondrial respiration: longer-lived species showed lower respiration under native cellular conditions (i.e. ROUTINE), but not at maximum fluxes (i.e. OXPHOS). Therefore, longer-lived species used a smaller proportion of their maximal capacity, indicating a larger spare respiratory capacity. Phylogenetic signal was moderate across the four respiration rates, and although mitochondrial traits were tightly correlated within individuals, they showed little evidence of coordinated evolutionary change across species. These results suggest that, in birds, lifespan is linked to how mitochondrial activity is regulated relative to capacity, rather than to maximal performance or efficiency per se, and point to the cellular control of mitochondrial respiration as a potential mechanism underlying the evolution of lifespan.
